To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
firefighters had an elevated risk of lymphatic/haematopoietic malignancy and brain tumours, and that the risk for lymphatic/haemetopoietic malignancies increased with duration of employment.
there were statistically significant excesses of brain cancers and leukaemia among young (< 40 years) and older (> or = 40 years) firefighters, respectively.
there is no overall excess of cancer among firefighters but there is an excess of brain tumours and lymphatic and hematopoietic cancers.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the risk of cancer among firefighters in these three cities was not increased.
there is no evidence that firefighters have a greater risk of death from cancer, lung disease or heart disease.
there is no clear evidence that exposure to fire smoke among firefighters leads to an increased risk in the development of cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of cancer among firefighters appears to be increased for brain cancer and lymphatic and hematopoietic cancers, particularly for younger and longer-term employed firefighters.
the risk of death from cancer among firefighters was no higher than the national rate, although there were some excesses of specific cancers.
there is a suggestion of a cancer risk among younger firefighters but the risk of cancer among older firefighters appears to be no greater than that in the general population.
The main takeaway from our work is that
firefighters have a higher risk of brain and leukaemia cancers.
there are no clear excesses of cancer or other non-malignancies in firefighters.
firefighters are not at an overall increased risk of death, although they do have an increased risk of brain cancer and leukaemia.
